name: Gareth Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual lineworker day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a power line crew for an electricity company and still check the truck before every repair. I am fifty-eight, and my two-year technical diploma helps when a drawing does not match the pole we find. I like showing a younger worker how to test an isolation properly; I dislike a report that calls the job done before the crew has looked. My partner and I have grown children and enough saved to cover more than six months, so we are starting to look at retirement without a firm date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that faster paperwork changes little out at the pole. I do not use AI tools, and I would still read a work order, test the line and sign only what we repaired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our higher lineworker pay, strong savings and plenty of nearby jobs make this mild future comfortable enough. A computer filing the form does not affect the wages from my physical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading my usual repair shifts and compare each work order with the pole tag before unloading. This year I would request a retirement income estimate with my partner and wait for the figures before setting any finish date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my living. A quick AI form will not change how my power line crew checks a live wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check the tag before unloading?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dispatch sheet can carry the next pole number after a long night, and moving the truck later wastes time. I read the metal tag at the site first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you set a finish date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a written income estimate that covers our ordinary costs and a talk with my partner about the hours we want. Six months of expenses saved is useful, not a lifetime income plan.

say: **Faster** paperwork leaves my crew’s physical isolation and repair work in place.
I would **keep** signing only work checked at the pole.
think: **Higher** pay, strong savings and nearby jobs make this mild future secure for us.
**Retirement** still needs a real income estimate before I choose a date.
do: **Keep** lead repair shifts and check work orders against pole tags.
**Request** retirement income estimate before choosing a finish date.
S0.quote: A quick AI form will not change how my power line crew checks a live wire.
fieldNote: He **avoids** AI tools and measures a finished job at the site.
Strong **savings** and higher pay support calm, while a retirement date still depends on actual household income figures.

steps.text: Keep lead repair shifts and verify pole tags before unloading
Request retirement estimate and defer finish date until figures arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI booking may help the depot, but somebody must answer when it sends a crew to the wrong pole. I would want the supervisor to keep a named dispatcher for awkward line faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office takes the early change, while my repairs remain physical. If a computer starts setting tight repair times, I would worry about safety more than my own pay because my crew has work and alternatives nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a month of wrong dispatch instructions and actual isolation times on signed work sheets. In the first year I would bring those sheets to the supervisor and ask for a correction contact, while staying on the normal repair rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about field pressure, not frightened for the household budget. A schedule cannot shorten a power line isolation by moving a number on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes on a wrong-instruction sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The order number, pole tag, isolation boundary and time the correction came back. A manager can then see exactly where the schedule failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the supervisor offers a software form instead of a person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the signed sheet to request a real call back on dangerous faults. I would not start using an untested AI tool to argue over a live site.

say: I would **demand** a named dispatcher for dangerous scheduling errors.
**Crew** work sheets should show actual isolation time.
think: **Office** tasks change first while my physical line shifts look secure.
**Tighter** targets could still pressure safety even if wages hold.
do: **Record** wrong dispatch orders and actual isolation time for one month.
**Bring** signed sheets to supervisor and request a correction contact.
**Keep** normal repair rota while schedules are tested.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed field targets, financially secure for now.
S1.quote: A schedule cannot shorten a power line isolation by moving a number on a screen.
fieldNote: His **resistance** is to trusting automated instructions, not to documenting errors.
His **own** pay looks safe, so the discomfort is about crew safety and accountability.

steps.text: Keep normal repair rota and record wrong dispatch orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 could change dispatch when I am sixty, and capable line robots around 2031 could reach our repairs at sixty-three. I would require a paid crew lead to check isolation and stop the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose high-paid callouts before I know whether retirement income is enough. We have more than six months saved and many nearby line jobs, but a robot taking a year of my wages would still change the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company this year for a written stop-work rule and request a retirement income estimate. In the first year after 2028, if line callouts fall for two months, I would compare written nearby lead offers while keeping my current crew shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible income cut, with enough cash and local options to respond. A line robot cannot be the only witness to its own failed power line repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What failure would make you stop the robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the machine tried to grip a split crossarm or moved past a marked isolation boundary, I would halt it. The crew would record the site before anyone restarted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire as soon as robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a written retirement estimate covers our living costs and my partner agrees on the timing. I would not leave a high-paid crew job because a robot is on a trial poster.

say: **Thinking** AI may change dispatch by 2028; robots could reach physical repairs around 2031.
A **paid** crew lead needs stop authority on robot jobs.
think: **High-paid** callouts could shrink before retirement income is clear.
**Strong** savings and nearby jobs give choices but do not replace a year of wages.
do: **Request** written crew stop rule and retirement estimate this year.
**Compare** nearby written lead offers if callout pay falls for two months.
**Keep** current crew shifts until a suitable offer or sufficient retirement income exists.
feel: **Anxious** about possible pay loss, with practical financial choices.
S2.quote: A line robot cannot be the only witness to its own failed power line repair.
fieldNote: He does **not** adopt the robot controls himself, consistent with resistance to new tools.
**Job** comparison depends on actual lost callouts and written nearby offers.

steps.text: Compare nearby written lead offers after two months of lost callout pay
Keep crew shifts until suitable offer or sufficient retirement income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2031 could alter plans when I am sixty-three, and capable robots around 2034 could climb when I am sixty-six. A few years should be enough to prove a physical inspection method before anyone signs a robot repair safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still need paid work at sixty-six if retirement income is short. I could take a hands-on inspection job because I know line hardware, but I would need at least the same wage and a real local opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company for posted inspection duties and pay this year. If it offers funded hands-on training and a local inspection vacancy matching my current pay, I would complete the course before 2031 and apply when the role opens; otherwise I would stay on line shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible field wage loss, though the longer notice lets me check a real offer. A field inspector should feel the cracked crossarm before signing a line robot’s repair safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the course make you inspect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A damaged pole and a work sheet with the wrong isolation marker. I would want a supervisor to show the trainee the real fault, not just a picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a desk inspection role suit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would keep line shifts rather than take a lower-paid screen approval job. I might change duties after physical training, but not abandon the part of work I trust.

say: The **longer** runway permits tested physical inspections before robots reach lines around 2034.
I would **sign** only repairs checked on site.
think: I **may** need wages at sixty-six if retirement income is short.
A **hands-on** inspector post needs comparable pay and a real local opening.
do: **Request** posted field inspection duties and pay this year.
**Complete** funded hands-on course before 2031 if matching-pay local vacancy exists.
**Apply** when posted inspector role matches current wage.
feel: **Anxious** about possible wage loss, able to check real terms.
S3.quote: A field inspector should feel the cracked crossarm before signing a line robot’s repair safe.
fieldNote: He would **learn** a physical inspection duty after proof and funded training.
His **pay** condition and actual local vacancy matter more than a new job title.

steps.text: Complete funded inspection course before 2031 if matching-pay local vacancy posted
Apply for posted local inspector role if pay matches current wage
Keep line shifts if suitable paid inspection path is absent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2036 arrives when I am sixty-eight and capable line robots around 2039 when I am seventy-one. If the retirement figures allow, I may have left full-time climbing before a robot takes a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have more than six months saved and a good wage now, but I cannot assume the income will cover a long retirement. I would still want younger workers to learn a real pole check before a machine plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep lead shifts now and update the retirement income estimate each year. If the figure covers our household costs by 2036, I would leave the electricity company job then; if it does not, I would seek a posted paid ground inspector role with enough wages to cover the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the distant machine date, careful about the retirement number. A line robot arriving at seventy-one cannot choose the year my partner and I can afford to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check from the ground?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare pole tags and completed work sheets with the actual hardware while a younger worker climbs. The role would need written duties and paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep teaching after leaving the company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might speak at one training day, but I would not promise free regular work. Our retirement plan would need to stand on actual income, not a hoped-for invitation.

say: A **decade** may let me leave full-time climbing before robots arrive around 2039.
**Younger** crews still need physical pole checks.
think: **Strong** savings and high pay do not guarantee a lifetime retirement income.
A **paid** ground role is a fallback if the figure is short.
do: **Keep** lead shifts and update retirement estimate annually.
**Leave** electricity company job by 2036 if retirement income covers household costs.
**Seek** posted paid ground inspector role if income is short and wage covers gap.
feel: **Calm** about later robots, careful with retirement arithmetic.
S4.quote: A line robot arriving at seventy-one cannot choose the year my partner and I can afford to stop.
fieldNote: His **conditional** exit is an actual leave-job choice, unlike merely asking for an estimate.
The **ground** fallback requires posted paid work that covers any household income gap.

steps.text: Keep lead shifts and update retirement estimate each year
Leave electricity company job by 2036 if retirement income covers costs
Seek posted paid ground inspector role if wage covers retirement gap

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable line robots around 2031 could cut high-paid callouts before our retirement figures are clear. A written crew stop rule and enough notice about hour changes would help. I have saved for a gap, not for a power line robot to spend my last working wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who will stand beside a machine on a live repair and be allowed to stop it. A good crew member should be paid for that judgment. The electricity company cannot call a screen safe simply because it has no reason to say no.

headlineQuote: I have saved for a gap, not for a power line robot to spend my last working wages.
portrait: **Gareth** is a fifty-eight-year-old electricity company crew lead with a technical diploma and a habit of checking pole tags before unloading.
**Higher** pay, more than six months of savings and many nearby lineworker jobs support him and his partner as retirement approaches.
He **never** uses AI tools, demands field safety accountability and considers a hands-on inspection path only after funded training.
He **may** leave full-time line work by 2036 if retirement income covers costs; otherwise he seeks paid ground work.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring line robots around 2031 and cut high-paid callouts before retirement income is known.
whatWouldHelp: A **written** crew stop rule and early notice of hour changes would help him plan.
